title: Kubernetes Networking Lab (Netlab)
description: Practice networking, firewall, and Kubernetes troubleshooting in an isolated Ubuntu VM with locally installed K3s and exercise images.

drills.title: Client interface is administratively down
drills.brief:
A user reports the client has no network at all. It cannot reach
the gateway, the server, or anything else.
drills.goal:
Bring the client back online so it can reach 10.10.2.10 and fetch
http://10.10.2.10:8080/health.

drills.title: Default route is missing
drills.brief:
The client can ping its own gateway 10.10.1.1 but cannot reach
anything beyond its own subnet. Attempts fail instantly, not after a timeout.
drills.goal: Restore reachability from the client to 10.10.2.10.

drills.title: Wrong prefix length puts the gateway off-subnet
drills.brief:
Someone edited the client network config by hand. Now the client
cannot even reach its own gateway, and adding a default route fails with
RTNETLINK answers: Network is unreachable.
drills.goal: Fix the client addressing so it can reach 10.10.1.1 and 10.10.2.10.

drills.title: Router is not forwarding packets
drills.brief:
After a reboot the client can ping the router (10.10.1.1) and the
server can ping the router (10.10.2.1), but the client cannot reach the server.
Both hosts have correct addresses and default routes. Nothing is firewalled.
drills.goal: Make the client able to reach 10.10.2.10 again.

drills.title: Stale static ARP entry poisons the gateway
drills.brief:
The client has a correct address, a correct default route, and the
router is healthy and forwarding. Yet every ping to the gateway times out.
Packets are clearly leaving the client -- they just never get an answer.
drills.goal: Restore reachability from the client to 10.10.1.1 and 10.10.2.10.

drills.title: Name resolves to the wrong address
drills.brief:
An application that talks to http://web.lab.local:8080/ started
timing out this morning. Using the IP address 10.10.2.10 directly works fine.
Nothing about the network path has changed.
drills.goal:
Make web.lab.local resolve to 10.10.2.10 again from the client, and
make http://web.lab.local:8080/health succeed.

drills.title: Lab hosts cannot reach a simulated WAN (missing MASQUERADE)
drills.brief:
Everything inside the lab still works: client to router, client to
server, HTTP between them. A separate local network namespace stands in for
an external WAN. The lab client cannot reach its test address because source
NAT is missing on the VM. No internet connection is required.
drills.goal:
Restore outbound reachability to the simulated WAN by putting
source NAT on the VM. Verify with: netlab exec client ping -c2 198.51.100.1

drills.title: A more-specific route swallows the traffic
drills.brief:
The client has a valid address and a valid default route via
10.10.1.1. It can reach the gateway. But traffic to the 10.10.2.0/24 network
fails instantly, and tcpdump on the router sees nothing at all arrive.
drills.goal:
Restore reachability from the client to 10.10.2.10 without removing
the default route.
drills.tools: ip route get, ip route show, tcpdump

drills.title: MTU mismatch: small requests work, large transfers hang
drills.brief:
Ping works. Small HTTP requests work instantly. But downloading a
large file from the server hangs after the first few kilobytes and eventually
times out. SSH connects, then freezes the moment output gets long. Classic.
drills.goal:
Make this complete within a few seconds:
  netlab exec client curl -s -o /dev/null http://10.10.2.10:8080/big.bin
drills.tools: ping -M do -s, ip link mtu, tcpdump, tracepath

drills.title: Default route points at a gateway that does not exist
drills.brief:
The client has an address and a default route, and its interface is
up. Pings to anything off-subnet fail with Host is unreachable rather than the
Network is unreachable you would get with no route at all.
drills.goal: Restore reachability from the client to 10.10.2.10.
drills.tools: ip route get, ip neigh, ping

drills.title: Default-deny INPUT with no rule for return traffic
drills.brief:
Someone hardened the client with a default-deny INPUT policy. Now
NOTHING works from the client -- not ping, not HTTP, not DNS. Yet tcpdump on the
server proves the requests arrive there and the replies are sent back.
drills.goal:
Make http://10.10.2.10:8080/health work from the client again WITHOUT
weakening the policy. The INPUT policy must stay DROP when you are done.

drills.title: Router drops forwarded traffic
drills.brief:
The client can ping the router. The router can ping the server. IP
forwarding is enabled and the routes are correct. But the client cannot reach
the server at all, and the packets vanish inside the router.
drills.goal:
Restore client to server connectivity while keeping the router
default-deny. The FORWARD policy must still be DROP when you are done.

drills.title: One service port is blocked, everything else is fine
drills.brief:
The monitoring system says the web server is down. But the host
pings fine, and the same server answers perfectly on port 9090. Only port 8080
hangs -- it does not refuse, it hangs.
drills.goal: Make http://10.10.2.10:8080/health work from the client again.

drills.title: The ACCEPT rule exists but never fires
drills.brief:
A colleague swears they added an ACCEPT rule for port 8080 on the
server, and you can see it in the ruleset. The client still cannot connect.
The colleague is now blaming the network.
drills.goal:
Get http://10.10.2.10:8080/health working from the client, while
leaving the server otherwise protected from the LAN.

drills.title: Egress filtering blocks one destination
drills.brief:
The client cannot reach the server. tcpdump on the CLIENT interface
shows no packets leaving at all, and ping reports an odd error rather than a
plain timeout. The server and router are both perfectly healthy.
drills.goal: Restore client access to 10.10.2.10 (ping and HTTP).
drills.tools: iptables OUTPUT chain, tcpdump, ping error text

drills.title: Port forward sends traffic to the wrong place
drills.brief:
The router is supposed to publish the DMZ web server on its own LAN
address: clients hit http://10.10.1.1:8080/ and the router forwards them to
10.10.2.10:8080. Someone set up the DNAT rule, but connections just hang.
Going directly to http://10.10.2.10:8080/ still works fine.
drills.goal:
Make this work from the client:
  netlab exec client curl -s http://10.10.1.1:8080/health

drills.title: Ping fails but the service is perfectly healthy
drills.brief:
Monitoring has paged you: the server is unreachable, ping gets 100%
loss. Users, however, are not complaining, and the web application is serving
traffic normally. Someone hardened the server overnight.
drills.goal: Make the server answer ping again, without breaking HTTP.

drills.title: The rule is hidden in a custom chain
drills.brief:
The client cannot reach the web server through the router. The
router FORWARD chain looks completely innocent -- policy ACCEPT, and no DROP
rules anywhere in it. Yet the packets never make it to the DMZ.
drills.goal:
Restore http://10.10.2.10:8080/health from the client without
deleting the LABSEC chain or its jump -- fix only what is wrong inside it.

drills.title: Build your first Deployment and Service
drills.brief:
Nothing is broken. This is the build exercise: you are going to
create a Deployment and put a Service in front of it, by hand, and watch what
Kubernetes does with each object.
drills.goal:
In the 'netlab' namespace, create:
  - a Deployment named 'web' running image nginx:1.27-alpine, 3 replicas,
    with pod label app=web
  - a ClusterIP Service named 'web' on port 80 targeting the pods
Success = 3 ready replicas, the Service has endpoints, and the toolbox pod
can fetch http://web from inside the cluster.

drills.title: CrashLoopBackOff
drills.brief:
A Deployment named 'crashy' was rolled out and the pod keeps
restarting. kubectl get pods shows CrashLoopBackOff and a restart count that
climbs every minute.
drills.goal:
Get the 'crashy' Deployment to 1 ready replica that stays running.
The container must keep running rather than exiting.

drills.title: ImagePullBackOff
drills.brief:
A Deployment named 'imgtest' will not start. The pod sits at
ErrImagePull, then ImagePullBackOff, and never produces any application logs
at all.
drills.goal: Get 'imgtest' to 1 ready replica running a real nginx image.

drills.title: Pod stuck in Pending -- unschedulable
drills.brief:
The 'bigapp' Deployment was applied ten minutes ago. Its pod is
still Pending. It has never been assigned to a node, there are no container
logs, and describing the pod shows a FailedScheduling event.
drills.goal:
Get 'bigapp' to 1 ready replica by making its resource requests
something this node can actually satisfy.
drills.tools: kubectl describe, get events, describe node

drills.title: Service has no endpoints (selector mismatch)
drills.brief:
The 'shop' Deployment is healthy: 2/2 pods Running and Ready. The
'shop' Service exists and has a ClusterIP. But every request to http://shop
from inside the cluster hangs or is refused.
drills.goal:
Make http://shop reachable from the toolbox pod. Do not delete the
Deployment -- fix the wiring.

drills.title: Pods Running but never Ready (bad readiness probe)
drills.brief:
The 'probeapp' pods show STATUS Running but READY 0/2. The
Deployment never reports itself available, the rollout hangs, and the Service
has no endpoints. The container itself is not restarting.
drills.goal:
Get 'probeapp' to 2 ready replicas with a working readiness probe,
and http://probeapp reachable from the toolbox pod. Keep a readiness probe --
do not just delete it.

drills.title: Missing ConfigMap and Secret
drills.brief:
The 'cfgapp' Deployment is stuck. The pod never reaches Running --
it sits in ContainerCreating or CreateContainerConfigError. There are no
application logs because the container was never created.
drills.goal:
Create the configuration the Deployment expects so the pod runs:
  - a ConfigMap named 'app-config' with key GREETING = hello-netlab
  - a Secret named 'app-secret' with key token = example-only-token
Success = pod Running, GREETING visible in its environment, and the ConfigMap
mounted at /etc/appconfig.
drills.tools: kubectl create configmap/secret, describe pod, exec

drills.title: A bad deploy is stuck mid-rollout -- roll it back
drills.brief:
Someone pushed a new image tag to the 'api' Deployment ten minutes
ago. The rollout never finished. The old pods are still serving traffic (good),
but a new pod is stuck failing to start and the deploy is frozen. Your job is
to get back to a known-good state fast, the way you would during an incident.
drills.goal:
Return 'api' to 2 ready replicas running the previous, working
nginx:1.27-alpine image.

drills.title: NetworkPolicy is blocking legitimate traffic
drills.brief:
The 'secure' Deployment is healthy: 2/2 Ready, and its Service has
endpoints. DNS resolves. Yet the toolbox pod cannot reach http://secure at all
-- the connection just hangs. A security change went in yesterday.
drills.goal:
Let the toolbox pod (label role=toolbox) reach the 'secure' pods on
port 80, while KEEPING the default-deny policy in place. Deleting the
default-deny is not the answer -- add a targeted allow.
drills.tools: kubectl get netpol, describe netpol, exec wget

drills.title: Expose a Deployment on a NodePort and trace it into iptables
drills.brief:
This drill joins the two halves of the course. The 'edge'
Deployment is running but has no Service. You will publish it on a fixed
NodePort, reach it from the VM itself, and then find the exact iptables rules
kube-proxy wrote to make that work.
drills.goal:
Create a Service named 'edge' of type NodePort, port 80, nodePort
30080, selecting the edge pods. Success = curl http://127.0.0.1:30080/ from the
VM returns the nginx page.
